title: Genotypic Specificity in Pea Under Increasing Salinity Stress
content: Pea (Pisum sativum L.) is an important grain legume crop with significant nutritional, agronomic and ecological value. Given the rise of salt affected soils and restricted water resources, improving salinity tolerance is becoming increasingly important. This study estimated the impact of increasing soil salinity on plant development and yield-related traits of five pea genotypes cultivated under controlled vertical farming conditions. Plants were exposed to four salinity treatments comprising a non-saline control (0 mM NaCl) and three salinity levels (100, 150 and 200 mM NaCl). The results showed that genotypes were the main source of variation for most observed traits, while salinity treatment also significantly affected several yield-related traits. Moderate salinity levels (100–150 mM NaCl) did not uniformly reduce plant performance and, in several genotype cycle combinations, resulted in numerical increases in yield-related and biomass traits. In contrast, the highest salinity level (200 mM NaCl) caused the most pronounced reductions in the evaluated traits, with maximum decreases of 42.4% in pod length, 73.8% in seed weight per plant, and 71.9% in fresh biomass. Genotype Favorit showed the highest overall stability, genotype Vilo exhibited the strongest decline in yield traits, while genotype Virtus exibited the greatest sensitivity in biomass under severe salinity. These results indicate significant genetic variability in salinity tolerance and identify promising genotypes for breeding programs and production in salinity affected soils and environments. Furthermore, the study confirms that a controlled vertical farming system provides a reliable, reproducible platform for soil salinity impact assessment and genotype evaluation, supporting the development of salt-tolerant pea cultivars.
